title: WhatsApp and audio misinformation during the Covid-19 pandemic
screen_reason: Quantitative content analysis of Covid-19 content donated by Portuguese WhatsApp users (988 files received 12-15 March 2020; 232 unique originals). Reports the share of the corpus classified as misinformation after a fact-checking/debunking pass (57.8%, n=134) and the share of audio files classified as misinformation (87.2%), both with stated denominators.

estimates.date: 12-15 March 2020 (content received by the research account over these four days)
estimates.measure_type: % of unique Covid-19-related WhatsApp content units classified as misinformation (inaccurate or incorrect) by the authors' debunking process
estimates.value_raw: misinformation represented 57.8% (n = 134) of the overall sample; non-misinformation 42.2% (n = 98); 134/232 original files
estimates.denominator: 232 original (de-duplicated) Covid-19-related content units forwarded to a research WhatsApp account by self-selecting Portuguese WhatsApp users, out of 988 files received (756 were duplicates)
estimates.definition: A file was coded as misinformation if the debunking pass found it contained either incorrect claims (false facts) or inaccurate claims (content misleadingly presented as truthful, or content still contested by science at the moment/place of collection, e.g. mask use); files with no false claims were coded 'nothing to register'
estimates.misinfo_def: "the authors adopted the concept of misinformation, differentiating between two levels of factuality: inaccurate or incorrect. In inaccurate content, authors included content misleadingly presented as truthful and content that, at the moment of data collection, to the best of scientific knowledge, was still being questioned (e.g., the use of masks)"
estimates.source_quote: The results of the debunking process (Graph 1) revealed that non-misinformation represented 42.2% (n = 98) while misinformation represented 57.8% (n = 134) of the overall sample.
estimates.page_loc: p. 6, Section 7 'Characterizing non-misinformation and misinformation on WhatsApp'; Graph 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two coders coded the whole sample with a codebook; Cohen's kappa 0.81 reported for claim type (no kappa reported for the misinformation variable itself). Debunking done by the authors through verification of facts against official sources, following Silverman (2020) and the IFCN code of principles; judged against the state of scientific knowledge at the time and place of sharing
estimates.moderator_quote: A message to advertise the research was published on the official social media accounts of the university, explaining the research objectives and inviting users to send information about Covid-19 received via WhatsApp. [...] The use of this technique fits well with the research objective, since its aim was to map the diversity of available content rather than carry out a probabilistic analysis of the research universe.
estimates.notes: Denominator is the DE-DUPLICATED corpus (232 originals), so this is a share of distinct items, not a share of share-events; coded CONTENT rather than SHARING for that reason (a SHARING content_share reading would want the 988 received files, for which no misinformation split is given). Self-selected donation corpus, explicitly non-probabilistic - the authors themselves warn the content 'may have originated from a set of more proactive individuals'. This prevalence therefore describes the donated corpus, not WhatsApp traffic in Portugal. Graph 1 gives the same measure per day (12-15 March); the overall figure is the collapsed representative point used here. Numerator is broad: it includes true-but-misleadingly-framed content and claims merely contested at the time, hence breadth=misleading.

estimates.measure_type: % of Covid-19-related WhatsApp AUDIO files classified as misinformation
estimates.value_raw: Of the total audio files analyzed, 87.2% were classified as misinformation (87.2% of 47 single-format audio files = 41 files)
estimates.denominator: Audio files in the de-duplicated corpus: 47 single-format audio files (Table 2; a further 4 files combined audio with another format, making 51 files containing audio)
estimates.definition: Same misinformation coding as the overall row (inaccurate or incorrect claims), restricted to files whose format was audio
estimates.misinfo_def: "all inaccurate or incorrect content available in the sample was considered to be misinformation"
estimates.source_quote: Of the total audio files analyzed, 87.2% were classified as misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: p. 8, Section 7 (audio subsection); denominators from Table 2, p. 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-coder codebook procedure and fact-checking-against-official-sources debunking as the overall row; kappa 0.81 for claim type only
estimates.notes: Format subgroup kept because audio is the paper's headline (it is in the title and is the stated novel contribution), not a demographic subgroup. Denominator is not stated in the sentence: 87.2% is an exact match for 41/47 (= 87.23%), i.e. the 47 SINGLE-format audio files of Table 2; it cannot be produced from 51 (the 47 single plus the 4 combined-format audio files: 44/51 = 86.3%, 45/51 = 88.2%). Value is verbatim, so kept under R8; the reconstructed count (41) is flagged as inference, not as a verbatim count.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted. (1) The inaccurate-vs-incorrect split exists only per day, in Graph 1 (March 12: 30.2% no misinfo / 16.3% inaccurate / 53.3% incorrect; March 13: 41.9 / 24.8 / 33.3; March 14: 46.5 / 32.6 / 20.9; March 15: 51.2 / 16.5 / 29.3). No overall inaccurate-only or incorrect-only share is stated, and summing across days would be a computed figure (forbidden by R8), so the strict 'incorrect/false' definition variant cannot be extracted. The daily series is collapsed to the overall 57.8% row. (2) Format shares (Table 2: text 42.8% single / 49.0% combined; audio 35.9% / 2.0%; video 18.3% / 7.4%; image 3.0% / 41.6%) are format prevalence, not misinformation prevalence. (3) 'audio was the most common among the content received and identified as duplicated, representing 85.6% (n = 694) of the total of the duplicate files received' - a share of duplicates that are audio, not a falsity share. (4) Topic/claim distribution (Table 1, n=435 claims: health-science 36.3%, policy and politics 21.8%, society 20.5%, pandemic 16.5%, conspiracy theories 4.8%) describes the topical mix of the corpus, not falsity. (5) Within-misinformation characteristics: 'misinformation ... using the "text" and "image with text" formats was present mostly as false references to a third party (71.4%)' and 'mainly directed toward the general population (63.6%)' - these are computed inside the misinformation-only subsample (would be within_misinfo_content=true) but no denominator count is stated for either, so they are not extractable to R8 standard. (6) Construct judgement: an argument exists for SHARING (content_share), since every unit was something a user had received and then forwarded; CONTENT was chosen because duplicates were stripped out of the denominator, making the unit the distinct item.

rob.design: Non-probabilistic donated-corpus content analysis. A research WhatsApp account was advertised on university social media and in a national newspaper, inviting users to forward Covid-19 content they had received; 988 files arrived 12-15 March 2020, reduced to 232 originals plus 756 exact duplicates. Quantitative content analysis (Krippendorff) with a codebook covering format, addressee, person, misinformation status and a claim typology; the whole sample was double-coded and Cohen's kappa for claim type was 0.81 (no reliability figure given for the misinformation variable). Misinformation determined by an integrated debunking pass verifying facts against official sources per Silverman (2020) and the IFCN code, judged against scientific knowledge at the collection date and place. No response rate or sampling frame exists by design; authors state the aim was to map content diversity, not to estimate the universe, and flag participant heterogeneity and possible over-representation of proactive senders as limitations. Intent was deliberately not coded.
rob.item6_quote: Depending on the result, a category was assigned to a file according to its meaning: (1) nothing to register, no false claims; (2) misinformation, contains inaccurate claims at the collected date/place; (3) misinformation, contains incorrect claims at the collected date/place.
rob.item10_quote: The results of the debunking process (Graph 1) revealed that non-misinformation represented 42.2% (n = 98) while misinformation represented 57.8% (n = 134) of the overall sample.
